## [Julie K. Brown](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/julie-k-brown)

A special citation is awarded to Miami Herald reporter Julie K. Brown for her groundbreaking reporting in 2017 and 2018 that exposed Jeffrey Epstein’s systematic abuse of young women, the justice system that protected him, and, over time, his powerful network of associates and enablers. Her Perversion of Justice series, published nearly a decade ago, revealed how prosecutors shielded Epstein from federal sex trafficking charges when he was first accused of abusing young women. She went on to document and give voice to the scores of victims who had been groomed and abused by him and others in his circle. Her work, and the release of the government’s Epstein files, continue to reverberate around the world.

## [Journalists and Media Workers Covering the War in Gaza](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/journalists-and-media-workers-covering-war-gaza)

In recent years the Pulitzer Board has issued citations honoring journalists covering wars in Ukraine and Afghanistan. This year, the Board recognizes the courageous work of journalists and media workers covering the war in Gaza. Under horrific conditions, an extraordinary number of journalists have died in the effort to tell the stories of Palestinians and others in Gaza. This war has also claimed the lives of poets and writers among the casualties. As the Pulitzer Prizes honor categories of journalism, arts, and letters, we mark the loss of invaluable records of the human experience.

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

**Sara Trevor Teasdale** (later **Filsinger**; August 8, 1884 – January 29, 1933) was an American [lyric poet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyric_poetry "Lyric poetry"). She was born in [St. Louis, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri "St. Louis, Missouri"), and used the name Filsinger after her 1914 marriage.[[1]](#cite_note-1) In 1918, she won a [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") for her 1917 poetry collection *Love Songs*.

## Life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sara_Teasdale&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Photograph_of_Sara_Teasdale_as_a_young_girl.jpg/250px-Photograph_of_Sara_Teasdale_as_a_young_girl.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photograph_of_Sara_Teasdale_as_a_young_girl.jpg)

Photograph of Sara Teasdale as a young girl

Sara Trevor Teasdale was born on August 8, 1884. She had poor health for much of her childhood, so she was home schooled until age 9. It was at age 10 that she was well enough to begin school. She started at Mary Institute in 1898, but switched to [Hosmer Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hosmer_Hall "Hosmer Hall") in 1899, graduating in 1903. The Teasdale family lived at 3668 Lindell Blvd. and then 38 Kingsbury Place in St. Louis, Missouri. Both homes were designed by Sara's mother. The house on Kingsbury Place had a private suite for Sara on the second floor. Guests entered through a separate entrance and were admitted by appointment. This suite is where Sara worked, slept, and often dined alone.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

From 1904 to 1907, Teasdale was a member of [The Potters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Potters_(artists_group) "The Potters (artists group)"), led by [Lillie Rose Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillie_Rose_Ernst "Lillie Rose Ernst"), a group of female artists in their late teens and early twenties who published, from 1904 to 1907, *The Potter's Wheel,* a monthly artistic and [literary magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_magazine "Literary magazine") in St. Louis.[[3]](#cite_note-stlouislgbthistory-3)

Teasdale's first poem was published in [William Marion Reedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Marion_Reedy "William Marion Reedy")'s *[Reedy's Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reedy's_Mirror "Reedy's Mirror")*, a local newspaper, in 1907. Her first collection of poems, *Sonnets to Duse and Other Poems*, was published that same year.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Sara_Teasdale._Photograph_by_unknown%2C_1907_Missouri_History_Museum_Photograph_and_Print_Collection._Portraits_n38637.jpg/250px-Sara_Teasdale._Photograph_by_unknown%2C_1907_Missouri_History_Museum_Photograph_and_Print_Collection._Portraits_n38637.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sara_Teasdale._Photograph_by_unknown,_1907_Missouri_History_Museum_Photograph_and_Print_Collection._Portraits_n38637.jpg)

Sara Teasdale, 1907 Missouri History Museum Photograph and Print Collection. Portraits n38637

Teasdale's second collection, *Helen of Troy and Other Poems*, was published in 1911.[[4]](#cite_note-4) It was well received by critics, who praised its lyrical mastery and romantic subject matter.

From 1911 to 1914 Teasdale was courted by several men, including the poet [Vachel Lindsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vachel_Lindsay "Vachel Lindsay"), who was truly in love with her but did not feel that he could provide enough money or stability to keep her satisfied. She chose to marry [Ernst Filsinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Filsinger?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ernst Filsinger (page does not exist)"), a longtime admirer of her poetry, on December 19, 1914.

Teasdale's third poetry collection, *Rivers to the Sea*, was published in 1915. It was a bestseller, being reprinted several times. In 1916 she and Filsinger moved to New York City, where they lived in an [Upper West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_West_Side "Upper West Side") apartment on Central Park West.

In 1918 she won a [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") for her 1917 poetry collection *Love Songs*. It was "made possible by a special grant from [The Poetry Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Society_of_America "Poetry Society of America")"; however, the sponsoring organization now lists it as the earliest [Pulitzer Prize for Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Poetry "Pulitzer Prize for Poetry") (inaugurated 1922).[[5]](#cite_note-pulitzer-5)

Filsinger's constant business travel caused Teasdale much loneliness.[[6]](#cite_note-6) In 1929, she moved interstate for three months, thereby satisfying the criterion to gain a divorce. She did not wish to inform Filsinger, only doing so at her lawyers' insistence as the divorce was going through. Filsinger was shocked. After the divorce she moved only two blocks from her old home on Central Park West. She rekindled her friendship with Vachel Lindsay, who was now married with children.

## Teasdale's suicide and "I Shall Not Care"

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sara_Teasdale&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Teasdale's suicide and ")]

In 1933, she died by suicide, overdosing on sleeping pills,[[7]](#cite_note-:0-7) and was interred in Bellefontaine Cemetery in St. Louis. Lindsay had died by suicide two years earlier.

The poem "I Shall Not Care", with themes of abandonment, bitterness, and contemplation of death, [was speculated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend "Urban legend") to be her suicide note to a former lover because of its depressing undertone.[[8]](#cite_note-8) However, the poem was first published in her 1915 collection *Rivers to the Sea*, 18 years before her suicide.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

I Shall Not Care

WHEN I am dead and over me bright April

:   :   Shakes out her rain-drenched hair,
:   Tho' you should lean above me broken-hearted,

    :   :   I shall not care.

I shall have peace, as leafy trees are peaceful

:   :   :   When rain bends down the bough,
:   And I shall be more silent and cold-hearted

    :   :   Than you are now.

## Legacy and influence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sara_Teasdale&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Legacy and influence")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Sara_Teasdale%2C_Sarony_Photo.jpg/250px-Sara_Teasdale%2C_Sarony_Photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sara_Teasdale,_Sarony_Photo.jpg)

Sara Teasdale, [Sarony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Sarony "Otto Sarony") photo, *Notable women of St. Louis*, 1914

* The poem "[There Will Come Soft Rains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There_Will_Come_Soft_Rains_(poem) "There Will Come Soft Rains (poem)")" from her 1920 collection *Flame and Shadow* inspired and is featured in a [famous short story of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There_Will_Come_Soft_Rains_(short_story) "There Will Come Soft Rains (short story)") by [Ray Bradbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Bradbury "Ray Bradbury").
* Teasdale is the favorite poet of Arlington LeGrande, the main character of [Jacquelyn Mitchard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacquelyn_Mitchard "Jacquelyn Mitchard")'s novel *The Most Wanted*.
* Teasdale's poems "The New Moon", "Only in Sleep" and "Stars" were set as choral pieces by [Ēriks Ešenvalds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ēriks_Ešenvalds "Ēriks Ešenvalds"), a Latvian composer, for Musica Baltica.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)
* "I Shall Not Care" from the 1915 *Collected Poems* appeared in the 1966 young adult novel *Up a Road Slowly* by [Irene Hunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_Hunt "Irene Hunt").[[12]](#cite_note-12)
* She was a major influence on academic [Marion Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Cummings "Marion Cummings").
* [Amy Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Beach "Amy Beach") (1867–1944) set Teasdale's poem "Dusk in June" to music.
* [Amy Aldrich Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Aldrich_Worth "Amy Aldrich Worth") (1888–1967) set Teasdale's poem "Pierrot's Song" to music.
* [Dagmar de Corval Rybner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dagmar_de_Corval_Rybner "Dagmar de Corval Rybner") (1890–1965) used Teasdale's poems for her songs "Pastorale", "Pierrot", and "Swans".[[13]](#cite_note-13)
* In 1932, [Mildred Lund Tyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mildred_Lund_Tyson "Mildred Lund Tyson") set Teasdale's poem "Like Barley Bending" to music.[[14]](#cite_note-14)
* In 1937, the poet [Orrick Glenday Johns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orrick_Glenday_Johns "Orrick Glenday Johns") wrote of her death in his book, "Time of Our Lives: The Story of My Father and Myself".[[15]](#cite_note-15)
* In 1967 [Tom Rapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Rapp "Tom Rapp") and the group [Pearls Before Swine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearls_Before_Swine_(band) "Pearls Before Swine (band)") recorded a musical rendition of "I Shall Not Care" on their first album *[One Nation Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Nation_Underground_(Pearls_Before_Swine_album) "One Nation Underground (Pearls Before Swine album)")*.
* In 1994, she was inducted into the [St. Louis Walk of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Walk_of_Fame "St. Louis Walk of Fame").[[16]](#cite_note-16)
* Teasdale's poem "There Will Be Rest" has been set to music under multiple titles by different choral composers. In 2004, [Craig Hella Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Hella_Johnson "Craig Hella Johnson") and [Frank Ticheli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Ticheli "Frank Ticheli") composed "There Will Be Rest" for the Conspirare choral ensemble. In 2017, [Z. Randall Stroope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z._Randall_Stroope "Z. Randall Stroope") composed "And Sure Stars Shining". In 2017, Elaine Hagenberg set the poem to music with the title "The Music of Stillness".[[17]](#cite_note-17)
